newsitem.title: UK: Mark crosses keep nerve at end of news-packed week.
newsitem.headline: Mark crosses keep nerve at end of news-packed week.

text.p: The mark barely broke a sweat on its European crosses in relatively quiet trade this week, a feat that has puzzled analysts given the welter of news out of Europe and the dollar's volatility.
"One element is the view the market can't concentrate on more than one issue at a time and the story this week has been the dollar," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in London.

A shortfall in German tax revenues, plans to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves, a Spanish rate cut and a gloomy outlook from the EU on Italy's hopes of joining the first wave of monetary union all failed to knock Europe's major currencies out of familiar ranges against the mark.

"There's been quite a bit of news this week and you would expect to see some shift in European currencies," said Elizabeth Legge, economist at Bankgesellschaft Berlin in London. "The tax shortfall in Germany was expected but it is still a bad number and it ought to be a major worry for EMU."
European markets barely flickered on Thursday's news Germany's tax revenue estimates for 1997 showed an 18 billion mark gap against spending.
Such a shortfall is seen taking the ratio of Germany's budget deficit to GDP above the 3.0 percent threshold target laid down in the Maastricht criteria.

And there was more cynicism than excitement over the German Finance Ministry's plans, announced on Thursday, to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves at a higher level closer to market value, with the prospect of using this windfall to trim German debt and eventually the deficit.

"The market still has the idea EMU is going ahead. There will be problems along the way but the feeling is that it's a political project, the economic risk has been taken out of the market," said CIBC's David Coleman.

Although Germany still adheres to a strict interpretation of the EMU criteria, some senior Bundesbank officials said this week sustainability of low deficits was more important than targeting 3.0 percent.
This was echoed today by European Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy, who referred to the EMU criteria as reference values.
The possibility of Germany missing the criteria raises the risk of a delay to the whole EMU project, which should send the mark soaring against its European satellites.
But analysts say market sentiment has opted for a flexible interpretation of the criteria, leading to a broad-based, timely EMU start -- and support for Europe's EMU hopefuls.

"I think Germany can live with 3.2 or 3.3 percent, it's becoming clear from what German politicians are saying they want it to start on time," said Jesper Dannesboe, economist at ABN-Amro in London. "We've already seen huge convergence in European markets, a delay now would be quite explosive."

Such EMU optimism has helped keep the lira on course against the mark despite a report early this week from EU finance ministers recommending Italy put in place more sustainable budgetary measures for monetary union.

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi reiterated this week his country's determination to be in at EMU's start.The government is expected to present its three-year economic plan to the EU at the end of this month which may improve its EMU hopes.
Mark/lira weakened by the end of the week, trading at 984.40/65 late on Friday against just above 990 early Monday.
The lira also found support in the prospect of lower Italian interest rates, reinforced by a rate cut in Spain earlier this week and in Portugal last week.

Both of these countries were praised for their economic plans at the same EU ministers' meeting that criticised Italy's efforts, raising market perceptions Spain and Portugal could be in the first wave of EMU.
By Friday afternoon, the peseta had risen to 84.20/22 per mark from around 84.55 early Monday.
The escudo was little changed on the week, recovering from fresh lows for this year hit on Thursday to trade at 100.65/70, similar to its levels at the start of the week.

The French franc, meantime, also made mild gains, mainly on the ruling centre-right's continuing lead in French opinion polls ahead of the May 25/June 1 elections. The franc stood at 3.3676/81 per mark on Friday against levels just above 3.37 francs early Monday.
-- Andrew Reierson, London Newsroom +44 171 542 6745
